questions.q: Why does Salesforce's Bulk API default to parallel mode rather than serial mode?
options: Because parallel mode maximizes throughput, which is the main reason to use Bulk API for large loads — serial mode is reserved for when parallel processing actually causes unresolved lock problems
Because serial mode is deprecated and no longer available
Because parallel mode is immune to record locking entirely
Because serial mode only works with Big Objects
questions.explain: Parallel mode is the fast option and the default starting point; Salesforce's own guidance treats serial mode as a fallback for when lock contention under parallel mode can't be solved another way, since serial mode trades away most of that throughput benefit.

questions.q: What is the recommended first fix for lock-timeout failures during a parallel-mode load, before switching to serial mode?
options: Immediately disable all triggers on the target object
Reduce the job to a single record per API call
Delete the skewed parent record entirely
Reorganize the load's batches to group records by their parent ID, so records for the same parent land in the same batch instead of being scattered across concurrently-running batches
questions.explain: Grouping records by parent ID when building batches sharply reduces how many different, simultaneously-running batches compete for the same parent's lock, which is the actual mechanism causing lock-timeout failures.

questions.q: At what level is Bulk API's concurrency mode (parallel vs. serial) set?
options: Per individual record
Per Apex trigger
At the job level — switching to serial mode means creating a separate, distinct job, not flipping a flag mid-job
Per Salesforce user license
questions.explain: Concurrency mode is a job-level setting, so moving to serial mode requires a separate job configured that way, distinct from the parallel jobs already running.

questions.q: Which operation does Salesforce's own guidance name as one likely to need serial mode from the start, rather than waiting for lock failures to prove it?
options: Updating a picklist field's label
Updating record ownership on objects using a private sharing model
Creating a new report type
Running a Query Plan check
questions.explain: Salesforce names ownership updates under private sharing, user creation, user role updates, and territory hierarchy updates as operations likely to need serial mode, because they touch wide-reaching shared structures that create heavy lock and recalculation effects.

questions.q: Why does this lesson caution against assuming sandbox testing fully predicts lock-contention behavior in production?
options: Because every org's specific data model, ownership distribution, and automation differ, so Salesforce itself can't predict in advance exactly when lock contention will occur — testing needs to reflect production's actual data shape and volume
Because sandboxes never run Bulk API jobs at all
Because sandboxes automatically disable record locking
Because Bulk API only works in production orgs
questions.explain: Lock contention depends on an org's specific skew and data shape, which a sandbox may not accurately mirror unless it's built to reflect production's real volume and distribution — a load that worked fine elsewhere isn't a reliable guarantee.
